findings.title: chunk throws RangeError for non-numeric and non-integer size alike
findings.detail: The guard at src/chunk.ts:2 throws RangeError for every rejected `size`, including cases where the argument is not a number at all (e.g. `NaN`, or `'2'` cast through an untyped/JSON path, which fails `Number.isInteger`) as well as fractional values. A RangeError conventionally signals an in-range value problem, while a wrong argument type is a TypeError; callers that pattern-match on `instanceof TypeError` to distinguish a programming error from a bad data value will misclassify `chunk(items, NaN)` as a range problem. Splitting the check (typeof/NaN → TypeError, non-integer or < 1 → RangeError) would make the two failure modes distinguishable. Behaviour is otherwise correct, so this is a low-severity API nit, not a bug.

findings.title: New exported utility ships with no test or usage reference
findings.detail: src/chunk.ts adds a public `chunk` helper, but the branch contains only that file — no spec/test file and no caller anywhere in the repository, so the boundary cases that matter for a chunking helper (empty input, `size` larger than `items.length`, exact multiples, `size` of 0/negative/NaN) are unverified and nothing exercises the function. Note the repo currently has no package.json or test runner at all, so this is a tracking note rather than a request to add an unrunnable suite: whoever wires chunk into real code should land tests alongside that first caller.

findings.title: New chunk helper ships with no tests
findings.detail: src/chunk.ts adds the only unit in the repo, and the diff includes no test for it. Its two boundary behaviours are the ones that get broken later by a refactor: a size that is not a positive integer must throw RangeError, and a size larger than the input must return one chunk. There is no test runner or test directory in the repo, so this is a suggestion rather than a blocker — add a small spec when test infrastructure exists, or at minimum record the expected behaviour in a doc comment.

findings.title: Tests leave the guard branches of parseSettings/pick uncovered
findings.detail: src/loadConfig.test.ts never exercises a top-level JSON primitive (e.g. '"x"', '1', 'true') nor a lookup of an inherited key such as 'toString' on a plain Settings object. Those are exactly the branches that make the code safe: the `typeof raw !== 'object'` check (loadConfig.ts:15) and the `Object.hasOwn` guard (loadConfig.ts:4). A regression that swapped the hasOwn check for a truthiness/in test, or dropped the primitive check, would pass the current suite, so these guards are untested. Adding one case per branch (string top-level, and pick({}, 'toString') throwing) closes it.

findings.title: pick() drops the settings source from missing-key errors
findings.detail: parseSettings threads `source` into every error it raises, but the settings object does not retain it and pick() has no source parameter, so a failure reads only `missing setting: <key>`. In a loader that composes several config files (the reason `source` exists at all), the operator cannot tell which file lacked the key. Concretely, `pick(parseSettings(read('a.json'), 'a.json'), 'port')` on a file without `port` throws `missing setting: port` with no file name. Carry the source (e.g. parseSettings returning a wrapper object, or pick taking a source label) so the error matches the diagnostics quality of the parse errors.

findings.title: Tests never exercise the inherited-key case that justifies Object.hasOwn
findings.detail: `Object.hasOwn` is used specifically so keys such as `toString` or `constructor` on a plain object literal are treated as absent, but the only missing-key assertion is `pick({}, 'a')`, which would also pass with a plain `key in settings` or truthiness check. A regression back to `if (!settings[key])` (which would also wrongly reject the empty-string setting `''`) would keep the suite green. Add a case like `pick({}, 'toString')` and `pick({ a: '' }, 'a')` to lock in both behaviours.

findings.title: pick() promises a string but can return undefined at runtime
findings.detail: `pick` only checks key presence (`Object.hasOwn`) and then returns `settings[key]!`. `Settings` is an exported `Record<string, string>` type, so nothing stops a caller from passing an object with an own key bound to `undefined` (e.g. `{ a: undefined } as unknown as Settings`, or a partial record assembled from optional fields). In that case `pick` returns `undefined` even though its signature says `string`, and the next use of the result (`.trim()`, `.length`, string concatenation assumptions) throws at the call site instead of at the config boundary. Validating `typeof value === 'string'` in `pick` — or reading through a helper that does — would keep the failure local and give an error that names the key and its source.

findings.title: parseSettings rejects a UTF-8 BOM instead of the settings it contains
findings.detail: parseSettings feeds the text straight to JSON.parse, which throws on a leading U+FEFF. Input: a settings file written by Windows Notepad or PowerShell's Out-File (both BOM by default), e.g. "\uFEFF{\"a\":\"1\"}". Wrong output: parseSettings throws "cannot read settings from f.json" even though the document is valid JSON, and since this function is the module's only text entry point, callers have no way to supply that file. Stripping a leading \uFEFF (or documenting that the caller must) would make the failure go away; Node's own JSON require path does this for comparison.

findings.title: pick's error drops the settings source, so failures cannot be attributed to a file
findings.detail: parseSettings takes a `source` and uses it in every message, but `pick` throws a bare "missing setting: a". With more than one settings object in play (the very reason `source` exists), the caller cannot tell which file lacks the key without wrapping the throw site itself. Passing the source through, or throwing a typed error carrying it, keeps the diagnostics consistent with parseSettings.

findings.title: No test pins the prototype-key behaviour that Object.hasOwn exists to protect
findings.detail: pick deliberately uses Object.hasOwn rather than `key in settings`, but the test only covers an own key and an absent key. A regression to `key in settings` (or to a lookup that reads the prototype chain) would let a settings object answer for keys such as "toString", "constructor" or "__proto__" and still pass the current suite; assert that pick({}, 'toString') and pick(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":"x"}'), '__proto__') behave as intended.

findings.title: pick's own-property guard is not covered by any test
findings.detail: The only non-trivial behavior in pick is the Object.hasOwn guard, but the added tests only cover a key that exists on the object and a key absent from an empty object ({}). Nothing asserts that an inherited key such as pick({}, 'toString') or pick(Object.create({a:'1'}), 'a') throws 'missing setting: a'. A regression that replaced the guard with `if (!(key in settings))` or `if (settings[key] === undefined)` would still pass the suite while letting a caller read a value off Object.prototype instead of failing on a genuinely missing setting. Add a case for an inherited key.

findings.title: parseSettings returns the JSON-parsed object as-is, so an own `__proto__` key survives validation
findings.detail: `parseSettings('{"__proto__":"x"}', 'f.json')` passes validation (the value is a string) and `return raw as Settings` hands back an object carrying an own `__proto__` property. This is not exploitable through the code in this diff: `pick` uses `Object.hasOwn`, so an inherited key still throws `missing setting`, and spreading copies `__proto__` as a plain data property. But the object is returned typed as `Settings`, so any future consumer that does `Object.assign({}, settings)` or a `for..in`-style merge would hit the `__proto__` setter and mutate the target's prototype. Building a fresh `Settings` via `Object.create(null)` (or `Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(raw))` after the loop) and rejecting a `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` key removes the footgun at the boundary.

findings.title: No test covers prototype-chain or `__proto__` keys in either function
findings.detail: The new tests cover plain objects, invalid JSON, array/null/wrongly-typed values, and a missing key, but not the behaviour that actually depends on `Object.hasOwn`: `pick({}, 'toString')` and `pick({}, 'constructor')` throw `missing setting` rather than returning a prototype method, and a `__proto__` key in the input text is accepted. Those are the interesting edge cases for a settings loader reading untrusted JSON, and they are currently unverified, so a later switch from `hasOwn` to `key in settings` would silently start returning `Object.prototype.toString` as a setting value.

findings.title: New relative import uses a `.js` extension while the repo declares no module system
findings.detail: `src/report.ts` now imports `formatMoney` via `./money.js`, but the checkout has no `package.json` and no `tsconfig.json`, so nothing declares `"type": "module"` or `moduleResolution: node16/nodenext/bundler` — the settings under which `./money.js` maps onto `./money.ts`. Under TypeScript's defaults (`module: commonjs`, node10 resolution) the specifier `./money.js` is looked up as a real file and `src/money.ts` is not found, giving `Cannot find module './money.js'` at build time. The previous version of `report.ts` had no imports at all, so this is the first place in the codebase where the choice of specifier extension matters. If the project is intended to be ESM/NodeNext, adding the matching `package.json` (`"type": "module"`) or `tsconfig.json` (`moduleResolution`) makes the extension correct and self-evident; otherwise the specifier should be `./money` to match the default resolution the rest of the tree implicitly relies on.

findings.title: New import uses a .js specifier in a repo with no declared module system
findings.detail: src/report.ts now imports `./money.js`, but this repo has neither a package.json (no `"type": "module"`) nor a tsconfig.json, so nothing establishes NodeNext/ESM/bundler-style resolution. Under the default compiler settings (module commonjs, moduleResolution node10) the specifier `./money.js` has no `money.js` file to bind to at type-check time, and under a CommonJS runtime loader (plain ts-node) `require('./money.js')` would also fail to find `src/money.ts`. I could not demonstrate a failure because the worktree contains no build config or entry point to exercise; the concern is that the import convention is unresolved/unfrozen by anything in the diff. Using `./money` (extensionless) would be safe in every configuration the repo currently implies.

findings.title: formatMoney emits malformed output for non-integer cents
findings.detail: src/money.ts is added by this diff (the function body is carried over unchanged from report.ts, so behavior is not a regression), but the new exported entry point can produce corrupt-looking strings. formatMoney(10.5) computes whole = floor(10.5/100) = 0 and frac = String(10.5 % 100).padStart(2,'0') = "10.5", yielding "$0.10.5"; formatMoney(-10.5) yields "-$0.10.5". Since the function is now a public module API rather than a private helper, a caller passing a non-integer (e.g. a float amount from a parsed price) gets a nonsensical string instead of a rounded value or a throw. Consider Math.trunc/round of the input or validating Number.isInteger(cents).

findings.title: New relative import uses a `.js` specifier with no module config in the repo
findings.detail: src/report.ts now imports `./money.js` while the source file is `src/money.ts`. That mapping only works under `moduleResolution` `node16`/`nodenext`/`bundler` (ESM/NodeNext output). The repo contains no package.json or tsconfig, so nothing pins the resolver; if the consuming toolchain compiles this tree with classic `moduleResolution: node` (CommonJS), the specifier does not resolve to `money.ts` and the build fails with TS2307 "Cannot find module './money.js'". Worth confirming the intended resolver (or adding the config) so the extension matches it.

findings.title: Extracted formatMoney still mishandles non-integer or non-finite cents, now as a widely reusable export
findings.detail: src/money.ts copies the previous private helper verbatim, so there is no regression in renderRows. However, making it a module-level export invites additional callers, and the arithmetic only degrades silently: formatMoney(1050.5) yields "$10.50.5", formatMoney(NaN) yields "$NaN.NaN", and formatMoney(1e21) yields "$10000000000000000000.00" with no rounding/validation. If this refactor is meant to widen usage, either assert Number.isSafeInteger(cents) or document that cents must be an integer.

findings.title: New './money.js' import specifier cannot be validated against the repo's module setup
findings.detail: src/report.ts now imports './money.js', but the worktree contains no package.json or tsconfig.json to establish moduleResolution/module (or whether the code runs through plain tsc output, ts-node, a bundler, or a native ESM runtime). Under a TS-only ESM loader with no extension mapping the specifier resolves to a non-existent src/money.js; under tsc NodeNext-style output it is required. No change requested without evidence, but adding a build config alongside the new module boundary would remove the ambiguity.
